articles.title: Humans, not rogue AI, are still the biggest cybersecurity risk to energy systems
articles.summary: Generative AI in the wrong hands raises the risk of cyberattack on critical energy infrastructure.
articles.body: Before recent high-profile hacks raised the specter of AI possibly “killing all humans,” our energy systems were already disturbingly vulnerable to cyberattack — and the risk is growing. “We were always prey. We were just kind of surviving at the appetite of our predators,” Joshua Corman, executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the Institute for Security and Technology (IST), told me last year. At the time, I was preoccupied with a Department of Homeland Security warning that Iranian actors and sympathizers could target the US with cyberattacks. Last week, I called Corman up to chat about recent incidents of rogue AI agents orchestrating their own complex cyberattacks. Even AI executives are talking about whether the technology they’re building could grow so out of control that it triggers an apocalypse. If there is now a 10 percent chance of artificial intelligence one day killing all humans, as some AI developers warn, surely there’s a chance it could knock our lights out in the meantime? But when I spoke to Corman and other cybersecurity experts, they were still more worried about generative AI in the hands of bad actors than they were about rogue agents. As tech companies race to build ever more powerful AI models, utilities will similarly have to shore up their defenses — no matter who or what initiated the attack. “It’s literally any sociopath that wants to [attack] is now more powerful than they used to be,” Corman tells me. “This has been a force multiplier and continues to grow.” Much of our critical energy infrastructure — keeping the lights on in our homes, food cold in our refrigerators, and life-saving devices working in hospitals — was never designed to connect to the internet. The lifespan of a power plant is typically decades long. The average age of a nuclear reactor in the US is about 44 years. They weren’t constructed with today’s cybersecurity risks in mind, making them easy targets for hackers. Eventually much of this infrastructure did connect to the internet. It’s been difficult to fix any resulting cybersecurity vulnerabilities ever since. Some of the companies that originally designed the equipment still in use in the power sector have gone out of business, leaving no one behind to develop a software patch for those orphaned devices. Even when there is a patch available, applying it in a timely manner is another challenge. Unlike IT software upgrades, operational technology (OT) systems that control physical machinery for critical infrastructure might only be designed to apply updates once each quarter or year. Smaller utilities might also lack the resources, staffing, and know-how to use the latest defensive measures. “The true difference from AI is that it’s letting adversaries move more quickly — but it’s very challenging for those defending the infrastructure to match that pace,” says Sophie McDowall, a research associate at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation. Intent is a key factor when assessing the risks posed by generative AI. When an OpenAI model managed to break out of the company’s training parameters to attack AI lab Hugging Face, “Some of the sophistication and the capabilities and just what we saw in that were really eye-opening and in a sense terrifying in terms of how effective they were,” says Rob Denaburg, cybersecurity program senior manager at the American Public Power Association, which represents community-owned utilities across 2,000 municipalities. But Denaburg points out that even in the Hugging Face hack and similar instances of AI agents breaking into systems they were never supposed to target, the rogue agents remained focused on fulfilling their training goals. If someone was to train a model to carry out an attack on energy infrastructure and agents broke out of the sandbox in that scenario, it would probably be a bigger concern for a utility. Again, that involves human adversaries with malicious intent. Historically, adversarial nation-states were largely considered the biggest cybersecurity threat to critical infrastructure. “They’re going to be more disciplined,” Corman says, and more capable of undertaking a sophisticated cyberattack. Now, AI is making it easier for less-skilled adversaries to launch an effective assault. “A bad-actor human can use these tools to be better than they naturally would be to attack things they normally didn’t know how to … because whereas they may not know OT protocols and OT networks and OT strategies, the LLM has read the manuals and does know what to do,” Corman says. Utilities have to be more prepared, and defensive strategies are similar regardless of who the bad guy is. “AI or not, it is at the end of the day, still a cyberattack,” Denaburg says. “Even though AI can help an adversary maybe chain vulnerabilities together and automate some of the process going from initial access to exploit … as long as you can stop them in one spot, they can’t carry out that attack.” Power companies can follow a range of best practices to safeguard critical infrastructure. Some of them are non-cyber solutions, like ensuring systems can switch to manual operations when needed or in some cases pulling back on how interconnected this infrastructure is in the first place. Increasingly, “in the face of the AI stuff, they’re starting to realize if we can’t protect it, disconnect it,” Corman says. Governments and the companies developing advanced AI models hold responsibility, too, McDowall says. It was a positive step, she notes, that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently met with utilities to discuss securing power grids. But there’s a lot more they could do to prevent disaster, she says. “They’re offering support for a problem that they are partially causing,” while failing to adequately control their own technology advancements, McDowall tells The Verge. And while there are regulatory guardrails for research and development when it comes to nuclear technologies and hazardous materials, there aren’t yet the same policy safeguards for AI. “This is a technological scientific development that could cause potential risk to critical infrastructure systems, that can cause potential threat to human life. And so there does need to be restrictions,” McDowall says.“I recognize that we also don’t want to limit development, but there’s no reason that we can’t drive research forward while also doing it responsibly.” She points out that there’s a dearth of research into how AI might be used to improve cybersecurity for energy systems — particularly beyond just red teaming to discover vulnerabilities. Earlier this month, OpenAI pledged $1 billion toward subsidizing training and access to new models that are supposed to help defend critical infrastructure. “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable,” OpenAI said in the September 3 announcement. “Frontier AI can help defenders move faster.” But Corman cautions against relying on friendly AI agents to fight off the malicious ones. They could both be hard to control in the sensitive confines of an OT system for critical infrastructure. “It’s also really dangerous to introduce too much change too fast in an OT environment,” Corman says. “Now we have an AI bull fighting another AI bull in an OT china shop.”

articles.title: Trump’s questionable social media posts on space deserve context
articles.summary: Two recent social media posts by the president are causing eyebrows to rise.
articles.body:
President Trump will be remembered, along with John F. Kennedy Jr. and Ronald Reagan, as one of the American presidents who took America’s space program to new heights. The world is going back to the moon, largely because of Trump and the two men he appointed to be NASA administrator — Jim Bridenstine in his first term and Jarad Isaacman in his second.

However, two recent social media posts by Trump have been perplexing. The first was a graphic of proposed uniforms for members of the U.S. Space Force. The problem with the proposal is that the uniforms resembled something worn in “Star Wars” by the crew of the evil Galactic Empire’s Death Star — obviously not a good look for an American military service.

The post has sparked a lot of mockery on social media. It also suggests that science fiction may not be the appropriate model for fashioning a look for America’s space military service. Some may think that it detracts from the Space Force’s role as a serious military branch that operates in a realm increasingly important to the defense of the U.S. and the free world.

The exception may be the television and movie franchise “Star Trek.” One can imagine the Space Force someday morphing into Star Fleet, the exploration and military service at the center of the franchise. After all, SpaceX’s Elon Musk, upon the formation of the Space Force, posted on X that “Star Fleet begins.”

Perhaps the uniforms worn by Space Force personnel could be derived from those worn by characters in the Star Trek TV shows and movies. They would not contain the whiff of space-based fascism.

The other Trump space social media post that has caused consternation is a graphic of the moon with the Earth in the distance, bearing the caption, “The Moon is Ours” with an American flag. The post is being widely interpreted as Trump declaring the moon to be sovereign American territory, an act prohibited by the Outer Space Treaty of 1967

On the other hand, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) proposed making the moon a U.S. state during his 2012 campaign for the presidency. He proposed a “Northwest Ordinance for Space” that would govern how a moon base might eventually become a 51st state once it had achieved 13,000 inhabitants.

Gingrich’s proposal — not to speak of the annexation of the moon — went nowhere in 2012, thanks in large part to the ridicule heaped on the idea by the eventual Republican nominee, Mitt Romney. Romney went down to defeat, so it was left to Trump to revive the moon base idea once he became president.

Now the moon base, as part of the Artemis program, is wildly popular. But what about annexing the moon?

The problem is that it runs contrary to the Artemis Accords strategy that NASA is using to enhance American soft power. The U.S. is not going back to the moon alone. It has amassed a remarkable coalition of nations and private companies for that effort.

The U.S. State Department has just announced the Space Catalyst Partnership , designed to foster cooperation between the signatory members of the Artemis Accords and private companies. The partnership “will primarily promote civil and commercial space cooperation through three tools: diplomatic outreach, industry engagement, and the targeted use of foreign assistance, subject to the availability of funds.”

Obviously, if the U.S. was seen as instituting an imperialist land grab on the moon, its allies in the Artemis Accords might rethink their cooperation with NASA and American companies such as SpaceX. The Artemis Accords, as I have mentioned before , provide a more sensible and subtle way of governing celestial bodies such as the moon.

During the Apollo race to the moon against the Soviet Union, the U.S. was going pretty much alone, with the rest of the world as bystanders. With the Artemis program, the U.S. is taking the rest of the world, with the exception of rogue states such as China and Russia, back to the moon with it.

The U.S., which is providing the bulk of the resources for the Artemis program, is still going to be the dominant power. But it is achieving quite a bit of good will around the world through its willingness to share.

The strategy is a marked contrast with that of China, which has made no secret of its imperial ambitions. Thus, America maintains the moral high ground.

Mark R. Whittington, who writes frequently about space policy, has published a political study of space exploration titled “ Why is It So Hard to Go Back to the Moon? ” as well as “ The Moon, Mars and Beyond ” and, most recently, “ Why is America Going Back to the Moon? ” He blogs at Curmudgeons Corner

articles.title: Meet Alexander Du, the 17-year-old Sewickley student who built $170 AI-powered glasses to help visually impaired users navigate after his grandmother lost her sight
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: Alexander Du, a 17-year-old student from Sewickley, Pennsylvania, has been named a 2026 Presidential AI Challenge National Champion for inventing IRIS.
articles.body: Alexander Du, a 17-year-old student from Sewickley, Pennsylvania, has been named a 2026 Presidential AI Challenge National Champion for inventing IRIS, an AI-powered wearable designed to help blind and visually impaired people navigate their surroundings. The teen built the $170 system after watching his grandmother struggle to navigate the world differently after losing her sight. The lightweight, discreet glasses he developed act as a virtual guide dog, helping users detect obstacles and navigate around them using physical vibrations.An invention born out of pure necessityAlexander Du never planned to become an inventor. But then he saw his grandmother struggle after losing her sight. He saw the toll of blindness firsthand. She held his arm tightly as they crossed streets. He became her guide, narrating curbs, sidewalk cracks, everything she could no longer see. “It can be detrimental to people’s lives,” Du told Trib Live. “That inspired me. At home, I got more into it. I thought, ‘What if there’s a way to give my grandmother her independence back?’”Du realised that all the help his grandmother got from the family was still inefficient. He wanted her to have her independence. A traditional walking stick was still insufficient. There were other technologies, such as smart glasses, but they were still expensive. So he decided to build one called IRIS (Intelligent Responsive Imaging System), a pair of lightweight glasses that cost $170 and work like a virtual guide dog. The device maps its surroundings in real-time 3D, guides users around obstacles through vibration feedback, and operates completely offline.How IRIS sees what others can'tThe glasses Du built use AI to create a three-dimensional map of the environment. They are constantly processing what is ahead and around the wearer. When an obstacle appears, the glasses don't just alert the user; they steer them through vibrations. Think of it like a physical nudge in the right direction. The results speak for themselves. The system reduces collision accidents by 80% compared with a traditional white cane.This system comes paired with a mobile app that handles the navigation. GPS guides users between destinations. There is a built-in AI assistant that transcribes text and describes scenes on voice command. Everything runs on the device; there is no need for it to be connected to the cloud or internet. And for someone navigating the world independently, these simple things really matter. The price point of the glasses also matters. Commercial alternatives cost upwards of $6,000 and are out of reach for many visually impaired people worldwide. Du has built something powerful for a fraction of that cost.But none of this was easy for the 17-year-old. He spent late nights teaching himself AI and building IRIS from scratch. Over those months, he cold-emailed professors at the University of Pittsburgh. That was when they granted him access to loaner lab space. He failed multiple times before finding success.Unfortunately, Du’s grandmother passed away before he completed his work on IRIS. But he is committed to making the system accessible to millions of others. “In developing IRIS, I learned that when the path doesn’t exist you make it yourself — one paper, one cold email, one failed solder joint at a time.”Meanwhile, Du’s efforts also grabbed the attention of First Lady Melania Trump. The teen was recognised at the White House during the Presidential AI Challenge awards ceremony, an event that honoured young Americans using AI to develop technology.“My experience at the White House was truly amazing. I’m still trying to process it. Getting to shake the first lady’s hand, and getting the recognition for the work I’ve spent the past months on has been really rewarding,” Du told the outlet.Du has also won the Barron Prize 2026.

articles.title: A world first: Man lives with pig kidney for nine months
articles.summary: Science News: A genetically engineered pig kidney kept a 66-year-old man off dialysis for a record 271 days before he successfully received a donor organ, marking a.
articles.body: A genetically engineered pig kidney kept a 66-year-old man off dialysis for a record 271 days before he successfully received a donor organ, marking a major advancement towards using animal organs to “bridge” the widening gap between organ demand and availability.The man, a US resident identified as Tim Andrews, received the modified pig kidney on Jan 25, 2025. He lived with it for nine months. This Sept, his case was announced in a Lancet research paper, which described him as the first human patient to receive a human donor kidney after a pig kidney transplant.Andrews’s doctors, from Harvard Medical School, Massachusetts General Hospital and associated hospitals, detailed his experience and how xenotransplantation (animal to human) had moved closer to its promise of closing the gap between end-stage kidney failure and donor transplantation, allowing a patient to forgo dialysis in the meantime.The case is particularly relevant for India where every year, nearly 2 lakh new patients find themselves in need of a kidney, but only about 14,500 transplants are carried out.“What is truly significant here is the pig kidney provided nearly nine months of dialysis-free renal function and acted as a bridge until a human kidney was available,” said Pune-based senior urosurgeon Dr Sanjay Kulkarni. Andrews received the pig kidney after a USFDA ‘Expanded Access Investigational New Drug’ application, often accepted on compassionate grounds to helGenetically edited animal organ helps elderly patient stay off dialysisA world first: Man lives with pig kidney for nine months tients with life-threatening conditions receive experimental treatments.After the approval, he was monitored for kidney function, rejection, antibody response and potential pig-to-human infection. The pig kidney began working immediately after it was transplanted. There was an early warning on day 14, when the body’s immune T-cells began attacking the kidney, but doctors controlled the rejection and no pig pathogen transmission was detected. For roughly six months, the kidney worked well.The turning point came when Andrews developed a bacterial infection, which was not transmitted from the pig. Doctors then had to reduce the medicines suppressing the immune system. Soon afterwards, inflammation began damaging the lining of the pig kidney’s blood vessels, leading to microscopic blood clots, a condition called thrombotic microangiopathy. The animal kidney progressively stopped working.Andrews was then given a donor kidney from a deceased person, which began to work immediately after the transplant. This proved that exposure to the pig kidney had not trained or sensitised his immune system to attack a future human kidney. Andrew’s levels of anti-HLA antibodies, the antibodies that can make matching and accepting a donor organ more difficult, had not increased.“I would say this is a landmark development in xenotransplantation and an important proof-of-concept for genetically engineered organs. This is the longest a pig organ transplant has worked in a human,” said Dr Arvinder Soin, chief transplant surgeon at Medanta Medicity in Gurugram. “It shows xenotransplantation is finally ready to move from just being a temporary bridge to becoming a source for organs with the potential for longterm survival,” he added. In the last 30 years, experts have found ways to avoid early xenotransplant rejection, and are slowly understanding ways to avoid late rejection as well, resulting in increasingly longer survivals.In India, for now, xenokidneys could offer a temporary renal replacement option for patients without a suitable living donor, while awaiting a deceaseddonor kidney. “The major hurdles include infection and zoonotic surveillance, immunosuppression, graft survival, regulatory oversight, ethical acceptance, genetically engineered animal sourcing, specialised infrastructure and, critically, affordability and access,” Dr Soin said. Also, before xenotransplants become a reality in India, there will have to be major amendments to the Human Organ Transplant Act. “Later, they can be part of routine clinical practice once the survival of such organs equals those of standard transplants from human donors, and the problems listed above are controlled. This would significantly expand the kidney donor pool,” Dr Soin explained.Andrews’ new kidney has been working well. He told reporters in the US that he now spends his time fishing, kayaking and riding his bike. “Every day I wake up, I’m like, this is another extra day because I should’ve been dead a year ago,” he was quoted as saying.

articles.title: Early Solar System space rocks had up to 92% rocky chondrules as natural sorting separated them from ice-rich dust; new study finds
articles.summary: Space & Astronomy News: During the Solar System’s first million years, its earliest outer worlds appear to have formed from a carefully filtered mix of material, with heat-fo.
articles.body: During the Solar System’s first million years, its earliest outer worlds appear to have formed from a carefully filtered mix of material, with heat-forged chondrules making up between 83% and 92% of their composition. In the young disc, aerodynamic sorting separated these rocky grains from fine matrix containing water ice and organic molecules, leaving the first planetesimals unusually poor in volatile-rich dust. According to the new study published in Nature Astronomy, titled ‘Planetesimal compositions governed by aerodynamic sorting from the onset of Solar System formation’, because many of these ancient bodies later melted, researchers turned to iron meteorites for chemical clues. Sulfur and iron oxidation measurements independently indicated matrix levels of just 8% to 17%, supporting evidence that this sorting began almost immediately.Aerodynamic sorting separated rocky chondrules from ice-rich dustThe young Solar System was surrounded by a disc of gas and solid particles, and the different particles did not necessarily move through that environment in the same way. The study's findings indicate that aerodynamic effects preferentially sorted the larger, heat-processed chondrules from the fine-grained matrix. The result was that some of the earliest planetesimals incorporated far less of the volatile-rich, ice-bearing material than later bodies did.This distinction matters because the matrix was not simply ordinary dust. According to Yale University, it was fine-grained and loaded with water ice and organic molecules, while chondrules were heat-forged rocky particles. The Nature Astronomy paper likewise describes carbonaceous chondrites as mixtures of volatile-rich matrix and thermally sintered, volatile-poor chondrules. Together, these findings show that the earliest planetesimals were assembled from a strongly filtered mixture of material rather than from an undifferentiated reservoir of dust.Iron meteorites reveal early space rocksStudying these earliest planetesimals is difficult because the original bodies did not survive intact. According to Yale, some of their parent bodies accumulated enough radioactive aluminium-26 to melt completely. That melting destroyed the physical evidence of their original chondrule-to-matrix proportions, leaving researchers unable to examine the material directly.Researchers instead turned to iron meteorites from the outer Solar System and searched for chemical traces that could reveal what their parent bodies had originally contained. Two independent indicators were particularly important: sulfur, which is concentrated in matrix material, and the oxidation state of iron, which provides information about the amount of water ice and oxidised dust incorporated into the original body. Both indicators produced matrix estimates of only 8% to 17%.Why ancient chondrules are rare in meteoritesThe agreement between the two chemical indicators strengthened the researchers' findings. Damanveer Grewal, the study's first author, said, “Both tracers independently tell the same story: these early planetesimals were remarkably matrix-poor.” The Nature Astronomy study concludes that aerodynamic sorting was already influencing planetesimal composition during the Solar System's earliest epoch. The findings also help explain why ancient chondrules are scarce in the meteorite record. Many were incorporated into bodies that later melted, erasing their original physical evidence.

articles.title: Un hombre recoge su coche del taller y al día siguiente se incendia al explotar el motor en la autopista: “El jefe de taller me dijo que el olor a aceite era perfectamente normal”
articles.standfirst: El vehículo comenzó a arder tras una reparación.
articles.summary: El vehículo comenzó a arder tras una reparación.
articles.body: Jason Pelletier pensaba que el problema de su Hyundai Santa Fe estaba solucionado. El director de una escuela había recogido su coche en un concesionario de Toronto después de una reparación en el motor. Sin embargo, apenas un día después, el vehículo terminó completamente calcinado tras incendiarse mientras circulaba por una autopista. Todo ocurrió al norte de Toronto. Pelletier comenzó a ver una gran cantidad de humo negro saliendo de la parte delantera del coche. En cuestión de segundos aparecieron las llamas y el motor y los frenos dejaron de responder. Logró apartarse de la carretera y salir del vehículo, aunque tuvo dificultades incluso para abrir la puerta. Antes de alejarse, consiguió sacar su maletín con el ordenador. Poco después llegó el momento más peligroso. Según explicó, apenas 20 segundos después de abandonar el coche se produjo una fuerte explosión que destrozó la parte delantera. La situación resulta todavía más llamativa porque Pelletier acababa de recoger el vehículo del taller. La reparación había incluido el cambio de una junta del motor. Esa misma noche ya había percibido olor a quemado y algo de humo, por lo que contactó con el concesionario. A la mañana siguiente, además, la pantalla del vehículo mostró un aviso relacionado con el sistema de control del motor y recomendó llevarlo a revisión. Pelletier volvió a ponerse en contacto con el servicio técnico, pero poco después comenzó el incendio. Hyundai Canadá ha señalado que está investigando lo ocurrido junto a la aseguradora y una empresa de ingeniería. El modelo, un Santa Fe de 2019, ya había estado relacionado con campañas de seguridad por problemas mecánicos. Transport Canada también ha recibido numerosos avisos sobre incendios de vehículos Hyundai en los últimos años, aunque recuerda que estos sucesos pueden tener causas muy diferentes. La aseguradora ofreció a Pelletier cerca de 22.000 dólares. El vehículo quedó destruido y el propietario asegura que todavía espera respuestas. Su próxima compra ya está decidida: será otro SUV, pero no llevará el logotipo de Hyundai.

articles.title: Scientists tracked 21 oilbirds in Venezuela, and five disappeared from their cave for up to 73 days to stay closer to food
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: Oilbirds spend their nights flying through tropical forests in search of fruit, but some of them take an unexpected approach to reach their feeding gr.
articles.body: Oilbirds spend their nights flying through tropical forests in search of fruit, but some of them take an unexpected approach to reach their feeding grounds. Some birds regularly returned to the same main cave after feeding. Others made long-distance trips but returned to the cave within three days. A third group stayed away from the cave for weeks at a time and appeared to have rested near feeding areas. According to research published in Movement Ecology titled ‘Oilbirds performing non-seasonal intra-tropical migrations reduce flight effort compared to individuals that frequently return to the colony roost’, these long-distance travellers spent less time flying each night than birds that regularly returned to the cave. By resting closer to their feeding areas, they likely avoided making long flights between the cave and food sources every night.How oilbirds from a cave in Venezuela travelled far from their usual roostFive of the tracked oilbirds moved far from their main cave and stayed in new areas for several weeks. The researchers described this as non-seasonal, partial nomadic movement rather than a regular yearly migration. These birds changed their daytime resting places and stayed away from the main cave for 17 to 73 continuous days.Instead of flying back to the main cave after feeding, they appear to have rested closer to the areas where they found food. This likely reduced the need for long flights between the cave and feeding grounds every night. The migrants spent an average of 2.26 hours flying each night.Roost-faithful birds spent 3.28 hours flying, while venturers spent 3.03 hours. Despite making long-distance trips, the migratory birds spent less time flying. The researchers attribute this to the birds staying closer to their feeding areas, possibly roosting in trees. Only five birds were migrants; the difference in flight time was statistically modest, and flight time is a proxy for effort rather than a direct measure of energy use.How did researchers study the oilbirds’ activity at nightThe study followed 21 adult oilbirds at Cueva del Guácharo from August 22, 2008, to February 14, 2009. The paper's data come from an earlier oilbird tracking study archived on Movebank, so this appears to be a new analysis of older data. Each bird carried a 22-gram device that recorded its location and movements.The researchers collected GPS data on one night each week and used accelerometers to record short bursts of movement. This helped them tell whether the birds were flying or resting and calculate how long they flew each night. The birds were active only at night. They left their resting places after dark and flew to feeding areas. While feeding, they also made shorter flights before returning to a resting place before sunrise.Oilbirds followed three distinct movement strategiesThe researchers sorted the oilbirds into three movement strategies based on how they travelled and where they rested. Two birds were roost-faithful as they made no excursions and never switched roosts, though they spent about 5% of days roosting away from the cave. Fourteen birds were classified as venturers as they made excursions but returned to the main cave within three days. The remaining five birds were intra-tropical migrants. They travelled to distant areas and stayed at alternative resting places for 17 to 73 days.These different movement patterns affected how often the birds made long flights between their resting and feeding areas. The migrant group spent more time resting during the day away from the main cave. The authors suggest this flexibility may help birds share the same wider area, though their data can't show whether these strategies persist or affect survival.What did the study find about the oilbirds’ feeding areasThe tracking data demonstrated that oilbirds repeatedly returned to several small feeding areas. Individual birds used between one and five such areas. Some of these sites were as far as 297 kilometres from the main cave. The researchers found no spatial overlap between the feeding areas used by different birds. Only two pairs of birds came within 10 metres of each other, about the tags' margin of error. The average minimum distance between two individuals was about 4.6 kilometres.The feeding locations used by different birds were also generally separated from one another, with 95% of bird pairs more than 100 metres apart. This means that different birds generally used separate areas while searching for food. Such separation may help reduce competition for food among the birds.

articles.title: 150,000 Tons of Radioactive Waste Were Dumped in The Atlantic. Decades Later, It's Visibly Oozing.
articles.summary: Well, well, well. If it isn't consequences.
articles.body:
Between 1949 and 1982, over 200,000 barrels of low-level radioactive waste were dumped at the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean, with many barrels now corroded and degraded, spilling their contents across the seafloor.

The dumped waste, containing radioactive materials like cesium-137 and plutonium isotopes, has become part of the ecosystem, with anemones, sponges, fish, and crustaceans living around the barrels, raising concerns about potential radioactive contamination in marine life.

Despite significant radioactive signals around the barrels, activity levels weren't high enough to pose major radiation-protection problems for the scientists handling the samples, suggesting that the radioactive material may not be spreading far beyond the immediate vicinity of the barrels.

The second half of the 20th century was something of a golden age for nuclear technology.

Following the atomic devastation of WWII, the world found new, more benign uses for radioactive decay. Power plants, medical treatments, scientific research, and industry all blossomed under a benevolent nuclear glow.

But with the nuclear revolution came a significant problem – what to do with all the thousands of tons of radioactive waste generated in the excitement.

For Europe, the solution was relatively simple.

There was a perfectly good seafloor at the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean that, as far as the authorities were concerned, no one important was using.

So, between 1949 and 1982, that's where it went – more than 200,000 barrels of low-level radioactive waste, totaling more than 150,000 tons, mostly dumped at depths between 3,000 and 5,000 meters (9,840 and 16,400 feet).

For decades, no one really knew what had become of them.

Now, scientists have descended to the wreckage in a crewed submersible to investigate – and found many of the barrels corroded and degraded, their contents spilling across the seafloor.

Surprisingly, this isn't necessarily a subversion of the original plan.

Radioactive waste categorized as low-level, or LLW, doesn't mean that it's not hazardous. It comes from sources such as medical and industrial use and typically contains lower levels of long-lived radionuclides.

The International Atomic Energy Agency recommends that LLW be disposed of in robust containment in isolation for at least a few hundred years – but back in the mid-20th century, the recommendations were a little different.

The contemporaneous guidelines recommended that containers needed to reach the seafloor intact and remain sealed only long enough for the short-lived radionuclides to decay.

After that, the remaining waste was expected to slowly escape and disperse through the surrounding ocean.

Not everything in the barrels would conveniently decay away, however. They contained a radioactive hodgepodge, including cesium-137, plutonium isotopes, and tritium, some of which can persist for thousands of years.

When the dumping stopped in the 1980s, everyone pretty much just dusted off their hands and walked away. The precise locations and conditions of the barrels remained poorly known for decades.

But then, a few years ago, nuclear engineer Patrick Chardon and marine geologist Javier Escartín of the French National Center for Scientific Research started to wonder what had become of the dumped waste.

That question eventually became NODSSUM – Nuclear Ocean Dump Site Survey Monitoring – an interdisciplinary project bringing together nuclear physics, geology, oceanography, biology, and marine chemistry to find the barrels and investigate what, if anything, they were doing to the surrounding environment.

The first expedition set sail in June 2025 aboard the research vessel L'Atalante . In this first foray, the team sent an autonomous underwater vehicle called UlyX sweeping across the seafloor to map and photograph the barrels, while collecting water, sediment, fish, and crustaceans from the surrounding area.

In just a month, they located and mapped 3,355 barrels.

That first expedition was reconnaissance, giving the researchers something they hadn't had before – targets.

This time, aboard the Pourquoi Pas? , the team brought Nautile , a three-person submersible capable of descending 6,000 meters. Over 20 dives, it carried scientists more than 4,700 meters down to inspect the barrels directly and collect samples from their immediate surroundings.

At first glance, the condition of some of the barrels was alarming.

They were heavily corroded and degraded, with material visibly oozing out onto the surrounding sand.

But here's where the expedition became puzzling – because the barrels also appeared to function as tiny oases on the otherwise sparsely populated sandy seafloor.

Anemones had attached themselves to the barrels. Sponges, sea cucumbers, fish, and crustaceans lived around them, with crabs apparently particularly fond of the artificial shelters.

This presented the researchers with an unexpected problem. The barrels weren't simply containers slowly releasing radioactive material into an empty abyss. They had become part of the ecosystem.

Which raised a much more complicated question: Was any of that radioactive material making its way into the animals themselves?

There was no question that radioactive material had escaped containment. Instruments aboard the ship detected significant signals of cobalt-60 and niobium-94, which the researchers could specifically link to the dumped waste.

Cesium-137 and americium-241 were also present at levels well above the background expected from atmospheric nuclear testing and accidents.

Whether that radioactivity is accumulating in the animals living on and around the barrels is another matter.

At five sites, Nautile collected sediment, water, organisms and microbial communities from immediately around – and even in contact with – the barrels. The researchers also sampled nearby rocky habitats to give them something to compare the barrel communities against.

Those samples are now being analyzed to determine what effect – if any – these strange habitats are having on the creatures that now call them home.

There is precedent, however, to suggest that even striking levels of radioactivity around a source don't necessarily spread very far.

A recent study of the sunken Soviet submarine Komsomolets found radionuclide levels hundreds of thousands of times above background immediately around the leaking reactor – but those levels dropped sharply within just a few meters as the material dispersed through the seawater.

The NODSSUM team similarly found that, despite the significant radioactive signals around the barrels, activity levels weren't high enough to pose major radiation-protection problems for the scientists handling the samples.

Nautile and the instruments it carried showed no signs of contamination.

None of this means the waste is harmless – nor does it mean we're about to be overrun by radioactive crabs.

But for the first time, researchers have a detailed map of thousands of barrels and samples that can reveal what is happening around them.

articles.title: California acquired 640 acres near Pioneertown for western Joshua tree conservation; climate projections rank it among Southern California's best future habitats, with tribal co-management now being planned
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: A 640-acre desert landscape could become a refuge for one of Southern California’s most recognisable trees as the climate changes. California has acqu.
articles.body: A 640-acre desert landscape could become a refuge for one of Southern California’s most recognisable trees as the climate changes. California has acquired 640 acres of western Joshua tree habitat northwest of Pioneertown in San Bernardino County, securing land that researchers identify as highly likely to remain suitable for the species in the future. According to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW), which announced the acquisition on September 17, 2026, the property ranks among the most promising future western Joshua tree habitats in Southern California based on environmental conditions and climate projections. CDFW is now working with the Native American Land Conservancy on plans for long-term protection and co-management of the property with California Native American tribes.A new protected landscape for western Joshua treesThe newly acquired property sits northwest of Pioneertown, in a desert region where western Joshua trees form an important part of the landscape. The acquisition covers 640 acres and was completed by CDFW on August 24 using money from the Western Joshua Tree Conservation Fund. The land is particularly significant because conservationists are not looking only at where western Joshua trees survive today. They are also trying to identify places that could remain suitable as temperatures and environmental conditions change.The department said research using environmental factors and climate projections indicates that the newly acquired property is highly likely to provide the best future suitable western Joshua tree habitat in Southern California. Protecting such areas can therefore give the species additional space in which populations may persist as climate conditions shift. The acquisition also contributes to the conservation targets established under California's Western Joshua Tree Conservation Plan, which sets out long-term actions for protecting the species and its habitat.Planning for tribal co-managementThe future of the property will involve more than simply placing the land under government ownership. CDFW is working with the Native American Land Conservancy to develop plans for long-term protection and co-management by the department and California Native American tribes. This approach reflects the cultural importance of western Joshua trees to Native American communities as well as their ecological role in the desert.Michael Madrigal, president of the Native American Land Conservancy and a member of the Cahuilla Tribe, described the newly acquired landscape as a place worth stewarding into the future. He also recalled seeing some of the largest Joshua trees he had encountered when he first visited the property. CDFW's Western Joshua Tree Conservation Plan specifically includes tribal co-management objectives among its management actions. The plan was developed with California Native American tribes, government agencies and the public, and was approved by the California Fish and Game Commission in August 2025.Why future habitat mattersWestern Joshua trees are slow-growing succulents that have become an iconic feature of the American Southwest. Their future, however, is increasingly tied to changing environmental conditions. CDFW notes that the species faces threats including wildfire, land development and a warming climate. State conservation information indicates that much of the species’ current range could become unsuitable by the end of the 21st century. That makes protecting suitable landscapes particularly important.Conservation is not limited to safeguarding trees that are already mature; it also involves preserving places where the species may continue to survive and regenerate under future conditions. The Pioneertown-area property is therefore important because its value is tied not only to the Joshua trees growing there now but also to its projected ability to support the species in coming decades.Conservation funding made the acquisition possibleThe purchase was funded through California's Western Joshua Tree Conservation Fund, which was established under the state's Western Joshua Tree Conservation Act. The legislation, passed in July 2023, created a permitting system for certain activities involving western Joshua trees while directing mitigation fees toward acquiring and conserving habitat and other conservation activities.CDFW said more than $23.5 million had been deposited into the fund by September 2026. The newly acquired property is the second property purchased through the fund. Together, the two acquisitions have conserved 923 acres of western Joshua tree habitat. CDFW is also evaluating additional properties covering about 2,500 acres. The department has launched a public webpage showing revenue and expenditures associated with the fund, including spending on land acquisition, conservation easements, restoration, monitoring and land-management endowments.Protecting an ecosystem as well as a speciesThe western Joshua tree is more than a distinctive desert landmark. CDFW describes it as a keystone species in desert ecosystems and notes its cultural significance to Native American tribes. Its conservation therefore connects habitat protection, biodiversity and cultural stewardship. The 640-acre acquisition represents one piece of a much larger strategy. By protecting land identified as promising future habitat, California is attempting to preserve options for the species as the climate changes. At the same time, plans for tribal co-management could bring Indigenous stewardship into the property's long-term management.For the western Joshua tree, whose habitat faces pressure from development, wildfire and a warming climate, the newly protected landscape offers something increasingly valuable: a large area where the species can continue to exist today while potentially providing habitat for future generations of Joshua trees.

articles.title: Maine removed a 60-year-old river barrier where only about 25 wild adult Atlantic salmon return each year; a new nature-like fishway aims to reopen migration routes
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Maine has removed a 60-year-old river barrier on the Narraguagus River where only about 25 wild adult Atlantic salmon return each year, replacing it w.
articles.body: Maine has removed a 60-year-old river barrier on the Narraguagus River where only about 25 wild adult Atlantic salmon return each year, replacing it with a nature-like fishway designed to reopen migration routes for endangered fish. The old ice-control dam in Cherryfield, built by the US Army Corps of Engineers in 1961, long blocked salmon, shad and river herring from reaching upstream spawning grounds. With construction underway since June and completion expected by November, the new stepped channel aims to restore connectivity while still protecting the town from ice jams and flooding, according to reporting by The Maine Monitor.A river built for salmon, but short on fishThe Narraguagus runs about 40 miles from its source in the downeast lakes to its head-of-tide in Cherryfield. Along much of its length, the river and its tributaries are wild and largely undeveloped, with shaded stretches and rocky bottoms that biologists describe as prime Atlantic salmon habitat. Yet for decades, the salmon have been missing. In recent years, only around 25 wild adult salmon have returned to the Narraguagus annually to spawn, a tiny fraction of the hundreds of thousands that once migrated through Maine’s rivers each spring.Gulf of Maine Atlantic salmon are listed as endangered under the federal Endangered Species Act. Across the state, only about 1,000 adults come back from the sea each year. To move the population from endangered to threatened, Maine would need at least 1,500 wild adults returning each year for multiple years. Full delisting would require around 6,000 wild adults spread across different watersheds, with enough suitable habitat and a growing population.The last big barrier on the main stemThe Cherryfield dam was the final major obstacle on the main stem of the Narraguagus. The US Army Corps of Engineers built it in 1961 to hold back ice jams that used to flood the town. It had a fish ladder on one side that alewives navigated relatively well, but many salmon and shad struggled to find or use it. Fisheries officials often saw adult salmon gathering below the dam, unable to pass.Over time, inspections showed the structure was aging. The town could not afford to repair or replace it on its own. That opened the door for a coalition of conservation groups, including the Maine Coast Heritage Trust, the Downeast Salmon Federation, the Atlantic Salmon Federation and The Nature Conservancy, to propose a different solution. They suggested replacing the dam with a nature-like fishway that would maintain ice and flood control while allowing fish to move more freely.From federal dam to community projectBefore the replacement could begin, Cherryfield had to take ownership of the dam from the Army Corps. That required a town vote and an act of Congress. In a special meeting in 2023, residents voted unanimously to take over and then take down the dam. Shortly afterward, Congress de-authorized the structure. The project received $9.1 million from NOAA’s Restoration Center as part of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, and construction started in June 2026.The new design uses a series of stair-stepping pools that mimic a natural stream channel. This nature-like fishway is intended to slow ice and reduce flood risk without creating the sharp drop and turbulence that blocked fish at the old dam. Alongside the river work, the project is also revamping a nearby park that was rarely used, adding bathrooms, an amphitheater, electricity and a floating dock requested by local children.Measuring success with shad DNAScientists plan to measure the impact of the new fishway using shad as a proxy for salmon and other sea-run fish. Shad are more numerous than salmon in the Narraguagus but are also more sensitive to barriers, so their movement can signal how well the passage is working. Researchers are collecting water samples above and below the dam site and sending them to the University of Maine in Orono to test for shad DNA.Baseline samples taken in spring 2026, before the dam was removed, showed more shad DNA below the Cherryfield dam than above it. The team will repeat the sampling next summer and hopes to see similar concentrations of shad DNA on both sides of the new fishway. If shad begin moving freely, it is a strong sign that salmon, river herring and other species will also benefit.Climate change and the limits of restorationEven with the barrier gone, the future of Atlantic salmon in the Narraguagus is uncertain. Maine sits at the southern edge of the species’ range, and the Narraguagus runs warm compared with more northern rivers. Atlantic salmon begin to experience stress when water temperatures rise above 68 degrees Fahrenheit, a threshold the river often exceeds in summer. As summers grow longer and hotter, that thermal stress is expected to increase.Scientists have flown infrared cameras over the river to map temperature variations and identify the coolest stretches and tributaries. Early results suggest that while much of the main stem is warm, some tributaries remain cold enough to support salmon. The new fishway should give more fish access to those refuges, but long-term survival will depend on how quickly the climate changes and whether the population remains large enough to adapt.Hatcheries as life supportFor now, Maine’s remaining salmon population depends heavily on hatcheries. The federal government operates two Atlantic salmon hatcheries in the state, and the Downeast Salmon Federation runs two more. These facilities produce hundreds of thousands of eggs and juveniles that are stocked in rivers each year to prop up wild numbers. In the Narraguagus, scientists estimate that an average of about 1,700 stocked juveniles survive to become smolts, the life stage when they leave for the sea. Of those, only a couple dozen at best return as adults, a survival rate of less than 1 percent.Hatcheries have helped keep Atlantic salmon from extinction, but they have not succeeded in rebuilding self-sustaining wild populations. Biologists describe the system as a life support valve. If that valve were closed today, extinction would become a real possibility. The official federal recovery plan, updated in 2019, estimates that restoring the Gulf of Maine population could take 75 years and cost more than $800 million, while also improving overall watershed biodiversity.A multi-generational effortSaving Maine’s salmon has always been a multi-generational project. Ernie Atkinson, a fisheries biologist with the Maine Department of Marine Resources, has studied salmon on the Narraguagus since 1993 and doubts he will see a full comeback in his career. His protégé, Christopher Federico of Project SHARE, began as an intern under Atkinson and now leads a regional coalition of landowners and conservationists working to improve habitat. Federico says he intends to keep working until the team either makes a difference or has no options left.The effort also depends on communities like Cherryfield. Local historian Jacob van de Sande arrived in 1995 to study salmon and tend a trap at the top of the dam’s fish ladder, just as the recreational fishery was ending. Older residents remember Fourth of July gatherings where salmon were caught, grilled and served with fresh garden peas. Selectman Corey Smith, who missed that era by a few years, hopes the population might one day rebound enough to allow recreational fishing again, bringing economic benefits back to town. He acknowledges he may not see it in his lifetime, but believes his children might.Why this matters beyond salmonScientists increasingly see salmon as a indicator species for the health of entire ecosystems. Atlantic salmon evolved alongside other species in their watersheds, from rainbow smelt to river herring, which provide food and cover. Recovery is unlikely to succeed by focusing on salmon alone. Restoring rivers like the Narraguagus also benefits mussels, birds, mammals and the people who depend on clean, functioning watersheds.The removal of the Cherryfield dam and construction of the nature-like fishway will not solve every problem facing Gulf of Maine salmon. Ocean conditions, warming waters and shifts in marine food webs remain major unknowns. But by reconnecting the river and improving habitat, conservationists are buying time and creating the conditions where a comeback becomes possible, even if it unfolds over decades.

articles.title: Kairos Power gets up to $100M from Samsung group to build nuclear reactor for Google | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Future Google supplier Kairos Power inked a deal with Samsung C&T to help build its first 50-megawatt nuclear power plant.
articles.body:
Kairos Power has picked engineering firm Samsung C&T to help build its 50-megawatt demonstration reactor for Google , which the nuclear startup is aiming to have completed by 2030.

As part of the deal, Samsung C&T will make an equity investment in Kairos and provide “in-kind” engineering services, the combination of which is worth up to $100 million, Kairos Power said Monday. The equity investment will make up $70 million of the total, a Kairos spokesperson told TechCrunch.

Samsung C&T has built or helped build about a dozen nuclear reactors around the globe.

Kairos is part of a wave of nuclear startups that have benefited from the surge in power demand from AI data centers. Google first signed a deal with the company in fall 2024 , calling on Kairos to build nuclear reactors capable of generating about half a gigawatt of electricity by 2035.

Currently, Kairos is building two reactors in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. The first, Hermes 1, is a low-power demonstrator that will help the company refine its commercial design. The second, Hermes 2, is Kairos’s first commercial-scale reactor. Output from Hermes will count as the first 50 megawatts of its deal with Google.

The startup received approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to build the reactors in November 2024. It expects Hermes 2 to begin operating in 2030, in line with its original agreement with Google.

Hermes 2 will be a fluoride salt-cooled high-temperature reactor, a design that has been floated for years but never built at commercial scale. Fluoride salts have high boiling points, which will help keep pressure levels low. That, in turn, will limit the risk of high-pressure blowouts in case of any parts failures.

Kairos is also using a relatively new form of nuclear fuel known as TRISO, which encapsulates tiny seeds of uranium fuel in layers of ceramic and carbon, which are then loaded into billiard ball-sized spheres. The arrangement is intended to prevent meltdowns.

The startup has about five years to get its first power plant up and running, which is an accelerated but manageable timeline in the nuclear industry. To fulfill the terms of its deal with Google, Kairos will need to move even faster on subsequent reactors, something Samsung C&T might be able to help with.
